newsitem.title: USA: Automation will not solve customs problems - U.N. official.
newsitem.headline: Automation will not solve customs problems - U.N. official.

text.p: As customs agencies in the Americas struggle to modernize, they should not expect automation to end all customs problems, top customs officials said here Tuesday.

"People think automation will end all bottlenecks, problems, corruption even," Benito Fernandez, a Honduran official with the United National Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said here Tuesday.
Customs organizations worldwide are in the midst of modernizing in order to clear cargo in a more efficient and speedier manner.

Shippers and carriers often complain particularly about customs clearance in Latin America, saying that antiquated systems and bureaucratic mentalities can leave cargo sitting at airports or seaports for weeks.
Speaking at the Customs/Trade/Finance Symposium of the Americas, Fernandez said that especially in Latin America, the automation process "could be rejected by customs workers."
"Many customs people feel that they will be replaced by a computer," Fernandez said. "These people need training and to be included in the process of restructuring."

Latin American customs officials also bemaoned the fact that in Latin America, customs jobs are for those with political connections and often the customs workers are not trained or qualified for their jobs. "It is a political bounty," Fernandez said.

Other officials said that as governments change every few years, the changes sometimes derail customs reforms. "We end up restructuring what has just been restructured," said one Latin American customs official.
On Monday, U.S. Customs director George Weise told the 1,000 delegates that the United States is moving from a transaction-by-transaction approach to an account approach to cargo clearance.
